title: Early Years Quality Fund Special Account Bill 2013
portfolio: School Education, Early Childhood and Youth

divisions.question: Ken O'Dowd I wish to speak on the Early Years Quality Fund Special Account Bill 2013, which I oppose in its entirety. This legislation seeks to establish a $300 million fund to provide wage increases to around 30 to 40 per cent, although this figure is not clear, of the long day care workforce and it only lasts for two years. As for what happens after two years, we guess it reverts back to where it is today. The centres will need to enter into enterprise bargaining agreements with staff and meet eligibility criteria. Given the limited pool of funds, it could be on a 'first in' basis, yet this is not even clear. After the two years workers will revert back to their previous wage. This would be history-making if this were the case. This bill is unbalanced. It is divisive, it is unfair and it will create a wage war. The bill has come around as a result of the union involved waging the Big Steps campaign, seeking to increase wages and conditions in the early childhood sector. The United Voice union—previously the Liquor, Hospitality and Miscellaneous Union, or the LHMU—have been campaigning for an increase in childcare sector wages since 2008, with their requests for increases ranging between $7 and $10 an hour. They proposed that the government fund this increase, and they were actually originally looking for $1.4 billion a year—and indexed. The coalition have a number of serious concerns with this bill. We do not dispute that childcare educators are low paid. We know these workers are skilled and work long and hard hours. Any wage increase should come through the Fair Work Commission, the body that the government has established with the responsibility of determining appropriate and fair levels of remuneration. Yet the United Voice union has refused to lodge a wage claim with the Fair Work Commission. Can you believe this? They rely instead on a Labor government to just hand over money hand over fist. It is unheard of. This $300 million is nothing more than an act of

The majority voted in favour of a motion to agree with the main idea of the [bill](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r5074). In parliamentary jargon, they voted to read the bill for a [second time](https://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html). the Senate will now discuss the bill in more detail. ### What is the bill's main idea? The [bill](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r5074) was introduced to establish the Early Years Quality Fund Special Account to: > *provide $300 million over two years to approved centre based long day care services in the form of grants to be used exclusively for the remuneration of employees and other employment-related costs and expenses.* Read more in the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1213a/13bd133).
John Hogg The question now is that the remaining stages of the bill be agreed to and the bill be now passed.

speeches.speaker: Sussan Ley
speeches.brief: Opposed the Early Years Quality Fund Special Account Bill 2013, arguing the $300 million fund would raise pay for only a minority of long day care workers while leaving more than 60 per cent behind, and accused the government of designing the scheme to boost membership of the union United Voice.

speeches.speaker: Kate Ellis
speeches.brief: Argued for the Early Years Quality Fund Special Account Bill 2013, defending the $300 million fund to raise wages for long day care educators through enterprise agreements, citing a further $190 million already invested in workforce qualifications, and condemning commentator Judith Sloan's description of educators as dimwits.

speeches.speaker: Jane Prentice
speeches.brief: Opposed the Early Years Quality Fund Special Account Bill 2013, arguing the $300 million fund would make only up to 40 per cent of the childcare workforce eligible for a pay rise while leaving providers without an enterprise bargaining agreement excluded, and accused union United Voice of using the scheme to boost its membership.

speeches.speaker: Kelly O'Dwyer
speeches.brief: Opposed the Early Years Quality Fund Special Account Bill 2013, arguing it bypasses the Fair Work Commission and pressures childcare centres into enterprise bargaining agreements to access $300 million in funding, and said only 76 per cent of women aged 25 to 54 are in paid work in Australia, compared with over 80 per cent elsewhere.

speeches.speaker: Bob Baldwin
speeches.brief: Opposed the Early Years Quality Fund Special Account Bill 2013, calling it a farce that will lift wages for only 30 to 40 per cent of long day care workers over two years, and cited reports that centres were told 60 per cent of staff must join the union to access the $300 million fund.

speeches.speaker: Dan Tehan
speeches.brief: Opposed the Early Years Quality Fund Special Account Bill 2013, criticising a seven-member panel that includes the United Voice union but no private sector representation, and noted the union has donated $7 million to the Labor Party over the last two election campaigns while family day care and occasional care are excluded from the fund.

speeches.speaker: Gai Brodtmann
speeches.brief: Supported the Early Years Quality Fund Special Account Bill 2013, citing a $25 billion four-year investment in early childhood education and care, wage increases of $3 an hour for Certificate III qualified educators, and research showing 90 per cent of a child's brain development occurs in the early years.

speeches.speaker: Craig Kelly
speeches.brief: Opposed the Early Years Quality Fund Special Account Bill 2013 as unaffordable, noting the government's cumulative deficits of $172 billion, and cited the Australian Industry Group's objection that conditioning funding on enterprise agreements is unfair and could breach section 344 of the Fair Work Act.

speeches.speaker: Alan Tudge
speeches.brief: Argued against the Early Years Quality Fund Special Account Bill 2013, accepting its wage-support objective but contending that it bypassed the Fair Work Commission, was rushed through parliament, benefited only about 40 per cent of childcare workers, provided funding for two years, and would increase costs for parents.

speeches.speaker: Rowan Ramsey
speeches.brief: Opposed the Early Years Quality Fund Special Account Bill 2013, arguing that a rushed inquiry and selective two-year funding would divide childcare workers and services, disadvantage regional and rural centres, and create higher fees, staff poaching, and uncertainty after funding ceased.

speeches.speaker: Nola Marino
speeches.brief: Opposed the Early Years Quality Fund Special Account Bill 2013, arguing that its $300 million fund would support only 30 to 40 per cent of long day care workers for two years, exclude many regional and rural services, create a two-tier system, and force centres and families to absorb higher wage costs.

speeches.speaker: Ken O'Dowd
speeches.brief: Opposed the Early Years Quality Fund Special Account Bill 2013, arguing that its $300 million fund would benefit only around 30 to 40 per cent of long day care workers for two years, create a wage divide, and improperly bypass the Fair Work Commission.

speeches.speaker: Michael McCormack
speeches.brief: Argued that quality childcare was increasingly unaffordable for families and that the bill's $300 million, two-year wage fund would pass further costs to families while attaching funding conditions concerning union membership.

speeches.speaker: Peter Garrett
speeches.brief: Summed up the Early Years Quality Fund bill, saying the government would invest a record $25 billion over four years in early childhood education, including $300 million over two years in grants to supplement educators' wages, and announced a new Pay Equity Unit within the Fair Work Commission.

speeches.speaker: Kate Lundy
speeches.brief: The speaker moved a motion to set the Senate's sitting hours for 28 June 2013 from 9:30 am to 3:40 pm, with specific time allocations for general business notice no. 1288 (relating to the Committee of Privileges) and for government business including the Early Years Quality Fund Special Account Bill 2013 and the Migration Amendment (Temporary Sponsored Visas) Bill 2013, each with limited debate time.

speeches.speaker: Matt Thistlethwaite
speeches.brief: The government introduced the Early Years Quality Fund Special Account Bill 2013, establishing a $300 million fund to support wage increases for early childhood educators and assist with implementing the National Quality Framework. The opposition argued the fund would benefit fewer than 40% of childcare workers, primarily served union membership drives, and created a two-tiered system.

acts.title: Early Years Quality Fund Special Account Act 2013
